solution:
The wrong pair is (1) 'Prabhakar' – Acharya P.K. Atre.

The chapter says that the newspaper 'Prabhakar' was started by Bhau Mahajan. It published the history of the French revolution and 'Shatpatre', the letters by Lokhitvadi (Gopal Hari Deshmukh), which aimed at creating social awareness.

The other three pairs are correct: Balshastri Jambhekar was the editor of 'Darpan', 'Deenbandhu' was started by Krishnarao Bhalekar, and 'Kesari' was started by Bal Gangadhar Tilak along with Gopal Ganesh Agarkar.

Newspapers were a very important medium of creating social awareness during the struggle for independence, and they are historical documents that record the events of their own time.

'Darpan', started in Mumbai in 1832 with Balshastri Jambhekar as its editor, and 'Prabhakar', started by Bhau Mahajan, carried writing aimed at social awareness such as Lokhitvadi's 'Shatpatre'. 'Dnyanoday' printed the news of the installation of the telegraph, of the starting of the railways and of the Indian war of Independence of 1857. 'Induprakash' supported widow remarriage in a big way, and 'Deenbandhu', started by Krishnarao Bhalekar, represented the masses of Indian society and tells us about the issues that concerned them.

'Kesari' and 'Maratha', started by Gopal Ganesh Agarkar and Bal Gangadhar Tilak in 1881, mark an important stage in the history of Indian newspapers before independence. They spoke about the social and political issues of that period, and Kesari published articles about nationwide situations, books in the native languages and the politics in England.

In this way newspapers spread information, shaped public opinion and supported reform, and in the 21st century the newspaper has been acknowledged as the fourth column of democracy.

We need mass media to make a free flow of information to all strata of society possible.

Editorials, various columns and supplements are essential parts of newspapers, and readers are also ensured a platform on which to voice their own opinions. In this way newspapers can help in making democracy stronger.

Radio broadcasts entertainment, awareness-creating and literary programmes, and special programmes for farmers, workers, the youth and women. Television is an audio-visual medium, and it was able to cross the inherent limitations of newspapers and radio by showing people the actual visuals of an event.

Mass media offers many professional opportunities to students of history.

Newspapers must provide fresh news and also unfold the background of an event, so they have to resort to history; reporters compare a news event with parallel events of the past, and newspapers run columns such as '50 Years Ago' or '100 Years Ago' and publish supplements and special issues on anniversaries, all of which need historical knowledge.

History is also essential in planning radio programmes. Akashvani has preserved recordings of the speeches delivered by the prime ministers of India each year on 15th August, invites historians as experts for discussions on anniversaries of national leaders and of historical events, and runs daily programmes such as 'On This Day in History'.

Television channels telecast programmes based on history. While producing serials of this type, accuracy in the presentation of environment, outfits, weaponry, life styles and lingual expression is essential, and that needs a deep understanding of the history of the period concerned. Channels like 'Discovery', 'National Geographic' and 'History' have opened a rich treasure of global history to the audience. People with deep knowledge of history are therefore sought after in all these fields.

The news or information carried by the media may not always represent the exact truth, so it needs to be scanned very carefully.

The chapter gives a famous example from Germany. 'Stern', a German weekly magazine, purchased a number of so-called handwritten diaries of Adolf Hitler and sold them to various publication companies. The diaries were verified for their authenticity and the news then appeared in print — but later those diaries were proved to be forged.

This shows that even information that has apparently been checked can turn out to be false, and that is why any information received through mass media must be reviewed critically.

A newspaper has to provide fresh news, but it also has to unfold the background of the event it reports, and for that it must resort to history.

While reporting news in detail, reporters compare the event with parallel events that happened in the past, and the past event may be printed in a separate frame so that the reader gets additional information and better insight into the current news. Newspapers also print columns of historical information under headings such as '50 Years Ago' or '100 Years Ago', which are based on historical documents or written history.

Newspapers further publish supplements and special issues on anniversaries — the chapter cites the centenary of the outbreak of World War I in 2014 and the seventy-five years completed in 2017 after the announcement of the 'Quit India' movement. Writing of this type is impossible without reviewing the history of the event, so knowledge of history is essential for newspaper articles.

Television is an audio-visual medium. Because it carries both sound and pictures, it was able to cross the inherent limitations of newspapers and of the radio and show people the actual visuals of an event.

The chapter says that so far there is no other alternative to television for watching an event as it actually happened. Its reach also widened steadily — the Delhi Doordarshan Centre was inaugurated in 1959, the Mumbai centre began telecasting in 1972, colour television was introduced in 1982, and in 1991 the government permitted private national and international channels to telecast in India, which made it possible for Indians to watch international events at home. For these reasons television is the most popular medium.
After Independence, All India Radio (AIR) became an integral part of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (India).
The Indian Broadcasting Company (IBC) was taken over by the British Government and named the 'Indian State Broadcasting Service' (ISBS). On 8th June 1936 it was renamed 'All India Radio' (AIR).
The 'Vividh Bharati' programmes are broadcast in 24 regional languages as well as 146 dialects of Indian languages.
AIR was named 'Akashvani' on the suggestion of the famous poet Pandit Narendra Sharma.
